headline.label: Drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1–4. It’s also preventable.
For every child lost to drowning, 7 more survive one and need emergency care. Kids like Adam.
More than 7 in 10 fatal child pool drownings happen at a home: their own, a grandparent’s, a friend’s or a neighbor’s.
Lower odds of drowning when a pool is fenced on all four sides instead of three. Layers work.

nonfatal.label: Emergency department visits for nonfatal drowning in the U.S. each year (2012–2021 average).
Nearly 4 in 10 drownings treated in emergency departments need hospital admission or transfer for more care, about 4 times the rate for all unintentional injuries.
Estimated ER-treated nonfatal pool and spa drowning injuries each year among children under 15 (2023–2025).

risks.title: When they slip away
risks.body: In a landmark CPSC study of young children who drowned in pools, 46% were last seen in the house, 69% weren’t expected to be at or in the pool, and 77% had been missing for 5 minutes or less.
risks.source: CPSC Safety Barrier Guidelines (study data from the late 1980s)

risks.title: When the house is full
risks.body: Parties, holidays and cookouts are when “everyone is watching,” so no one is. Doors get propped open, alarms get switched off, and a toddler can slip away without anyone noticing. Name a Water Watcher and keep every layer on.

risks.title: At someone else’s home
risks.body: Grandparents’, neighbors’ and friends’ pools count too. More than 70% of fatal child pool and spa drownings happen at a home, including the homes of family, friends and neighbors.

risks.title: In the bathtub
risks.body: Babies under 1 most often drown in bathtubs. Young children can drown in just an inch or two of water, so stay within arm’s reach at bath time and empty buckets and kiddie pools.

risks.title: In summer, and all year
risks.body: Pool and spa drownings peak in June, July and August. But bathtubs, buckets, hot tubs and ponds don’t take the winter off. Keep every layer in place in every season.

risks.title: Children with autism
risks.body: Children with autism face a much higher drowning risk, often after wandering. One study put their risk of a fatal drowning at about 160 times that of other children. Door alarms, adaptive swim lessons and a wandering plan save lives.
risks.source: Guan & Li, American Journal of Public Health, 2017

facts.label: Drowning is the leading cause of death for children ages 1–4.
facts.detail: It happens most often in home pools, and layers of protection help prevent it.

facts.label: Children under 15 lost to pool or spa drownings each year, on average (2021–2023).
facts.detail: Nearly 80% of them were younger than 5.

facts.label: Toddlers between 1 and 3 years old are at the highest risk.
facts.detail: They are newly mobile, curious, and drawn to water, but have no sense of danger.

facts.label: Lives lost to unintentional drowning each year in the U.S. (2020–2022).
facts.detail: That’s about 500 more each year than in 2019.

facts.label: Drowning is the second leading cause of unintentional-injury death for children ages 5–14, after car crashes.
Black children ages 10–14 drown in swimming pools at 7.6 times the rate of White children.
facts.detail: Access to swim lessons is a big part of that gap.

groups.title: Nonfatal drowning
groups.intro: Many children survive a drowning. Some recover completely. Others, like Adam, live with injuries that last a lifetime, such as brain injury or permanent disability.

facts.label: Emergency department visits for nonfatal drowning in the U.S. each year (2012–2021 average).
Nearly 4 in 10 drownings treated in emergency departments need hospital admission or transfer for more care, about 4 times the rate for all unintentional injuries.
Estimated ER-treated nonfatal pool and spa drowning injuries each year among children under 15 (2023–2025).
Drowning happens in seconds and is often silent.
facts.detail: There is usually no splashing or calling for help. Young children can drown in an inch or two of water.

facts.label: Of young children who drowned in pools weren’t expected to be at or in the pool.
facts.detail: And 77% had been missing for 5 minutes or less (CPSC study, late-1980s data).

groups.title: What protects children
groups.intro: The good news: drowning is preventable, and the layers of protection work best together.

facts.label: Lower odds of drowning with a fence that isolates the pool on all four sides, compared with three-sided fencing.
facts.detail: When the house is one side of the fence, a toddler can walk straight out the back door to the water.

facts.label: Toddlers and weak swimmers need an adult within arm’s reach, “touch supervision,” whenever they’re in or near water.
facts.detail: Name a Water Watcher so there’s never a question of who’s watching.

facts.label: Swim lessons starting after age 1 are linked to a lower drowning risk for young children.
facts.detail: The benefit is real but hard to size precisely, and lessons never replace supervision or barriers.

facts.label: Fast CPR with rescue breaths matters after a drowning. Our mom started CPR on Adam right away.
facts.detail: Take an infant and child CPR class, and renew it every two years.
